blocks.text: But here let everyone believe what he will. I, however, am fully persuaded that the land crocodile among most of the ancients was neither the skink nor a huge beast, but that very animal which, as we have said, is called צב tsab by the Hebrews, ܚܪܕܘܢܐ chardona by the Chaldeans and Syrians, and ضب [ḍabb] dhab and حردون [ḥardūn] chardaun by the Arabs [II, 484]. How it differs from the skink, these same writers teach us abundantly. That the matter is so will at once be noticed by anyone who compares the nature and powers of the two. 1. The blood of the dhab strengthens the sight. So in Pliny, book 28, chapter 8: the blood of the land crocodile, applied as an ointment, gives clearness of sight and remedies scars of the eyes. Hence Galen, On Simples, book 10, chapter 6: Εἰ δὲ τὸ τοῦ χερσαίου κροκοδείλου (αἷμα) ποιητικὸν ὀξυδερκίας ἐστὶν, οὐ δε πειράζειν ἔμελλον, ἔχων ὀξυδερκῆ φάρμακα δόκιμα· [Ei de to tou chersaiou krokodeilou (haima) poiētikon oxyderkias estin, ou de peirazein emellon, echōn oxyderkē pharmaka dokima] Whether the blood of the land crocodile sharpens the sight I had no need to test, since I had other proven drugs for that purpose. 2. But the ضب [ḍabb] dhab has more potency in its dung, by which white spots and cataracts are removed from the eyes. See this very thing in Pliny concerning crocodilea, that is, the dung of the land crocodile! It lives only on land and among the most fragrant flowers. For this reason its intestines are diligently sought out, stuffed with a pleasant scent. They call it crocodilea; it is most useful for defects of the eyes, applied with leek juice, and against cataracts or dimness. Alexander of Tralles too, book 2, chapter 5, wants the dung of the land crocodile mixed into an eye-salve for scars of the eyes and for wiping away λευκώματα [leukōmata]. 3. The dung of the ضب [ḍabb] dhab gives brightness to the face, removing spots, warts, scurf and freckles. The same is the power of crocodilea; Pliny: Smeared on with Cyprus oil, it also removes blemishes growing on the face; with water, all diseases whose nature is to spread over the face, and it restores brightness. It removes freckles and pimples and all spots. Dioscorides, book 2, in the chapter On the dung of animals: Ἡ δὲ τοῦ χερσαίου κροκοδείλου ἄφοδος ἁρμώζει ἐπὶ τῶν γυναικῶν πρὸς εὔχροιαν, καὶ στίλβωσιν τῶν προσώπων. [Hē de tou chersaiou krokodeilou aphodos harmōzei epi tōn gynaikōn pros euchroian, kai stilbōsin tōn prosōpōn.] Galen, On Simples, book 10, chapter 29: Τὴν δὲ τῶν χερσαίων κροκοδείλων τούτων, τῶν μικρῶν τε, καὶ χαμαιρεπῶν, κόπρον ἔντιμον αἱ τρυφῶσαι πεποιήκασι, γυναῖκες· αἷς οὐκ ἀρκεῖ τοῖς ἄλλοις φαρμάκοις, τοσούτοις οὖσι, λαμπρόν τε καὶ τετανὸν ἐργάζεσθαι τὸ περὶ τὸ πρόσωπον δέρμα. προστιθέασι δὲ αὐταῖς καὶ τῶν κροκοδείλων κόπρον. [Tēn de tōn chersaiōn krokodeilōn toutōn, tōn mikrōn te, kai chamairepōn, kopron entimon hai tryphōsai pepoiēkasi, gynaikes· hais ouk arkei tois allois pharmakois, tosoutois ousi, lampron te kai tetanon ergazesthai to peri to prosōpon derma. prostitheasi de autais kai tōn krokodeilōn kopron.] On this account Clement of Alexandria, in book 3 of the Paedagogus, declares the women of his time deserving to perish not [col. 1062] once but three times. Τρὶς γὰρ, he says, οὐχ ἅπαξ ἀπολωλέναι δίκαιαι κροκοδείλων ἀποπάτοις χρώμεναι. [Tris gar … ouch hapax apolōlenai dikaiai krokodeilōn apopatois chrōmenai.] Note especially that the words of Dioscorides just cited are rendered thus in the Arabic version in Ibn al-Baitar: خرو الحردون يصلح للغمرة ولتحسين اللون وصقال الوجه والبشرة [khurū al-ḥardūn yaṣluḥu li-l-ghumra wa-li-taḥsīn al-lawn wa-ṣiqāl al-wajh wa-l-bashara] The dung of alchardaun is useful for a liniment by which brightness is given to women, and the colour becomes more beautiful, and the face and skin more shining. Thus in place of the land crocodile there stands chardaun. And that chardaun is the same as ضب [ḍabb] dhab, or צב tsab, has been abundantly proved above ^{h)}). 4. The Arabs prescribe the dung of the dhab against alphoi, vitiligo and elephantiasis. So, on the authority of Paul of Aegina, ἡ τῶν χερσαίων [II, 485] κροκοδείλων κόπρος, ἀλφοὺς ἀποῤῥύπτει· [hē tōn chersaiōn krokodeilōn kopros, alphous aporrhyptei] And Aetius describes at length ^{i)} how the Indians use the land crocodile against elephantiasis. And Galen, in the place cited: Ἡ δέ γε τῶν κροκοδείλων κόπρος ὥσπερ τῶν προσώπων τὴν ἔφηλιν ἀφαιρεῖν πέφυκεν, οὕτω καὶ ἑλεῖν ἀλφοὺς, καὶ λειχῆνας. [Hē de ge tōn krokodeilōn kopros hōsper tōn prosōpōn tēn ephēlin aphairein pephyken, houtō kai helein alphous, kai leichēnas.] 5. Serapion, chapter 446, says word for word about the dung of the stellio the same things that Dioscorides and Galen say about the dung of the land crocodile. But there stellio in Arabic is ضب [ḍabb] dhab, or حردون [ḥardūn] chardaun. So too the old translators of Galen and Dioscorides everywhere use the name stellio for the land crocodile. By the same error the late Erpenius renders حردون [ḥardūn] chardaun in Luqman's Fables as stellio. 6. In Avicenna the ضب [ḍabb] dhab is a rare animal, almost peculiar to Arabia. So is the land crocodile, whose dung in Galen is ἔντιμον [entimon]; in Aetius, hard to find; in Pliny, diligently sought out. But Dioscorides states that skinks are found in Mauretania, Egypt, India and Arabia; Solinus says they are very numerous around the Nile. 7. Finally, there is no reason why the skink should be called the land crocodile, since it is an animal just as ἀμφίβιον [amphibion] as the larger crocodile, and lives mostly in the water. Nor are the same powers attributed to the skink and the land crocodile: of the latter no one, as far as I know, has written what all report of the skink, that its use rouses torpor of the nerves and extinguishes the force of poison. So that from this too it appears that they are different animals.
